name: The Tuatha De Danann: the god-people of Danu arriving in dark clouds
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The foundational anchor ladder for the whole Irish pillar (per SHARED sec 16 teach-before-test -- every downstream Lugh / Dagda / Morrigan / Nuada / Manannan ladder assumes the kid has met the TUATHA DE DANANN by name). T1: the TUATHA DE DANANN are the god-people of Ireland -- their name means 'the people of the goddess DANU'. They are the fifth wave of settlers to arrive in Ireland in the Lebor Gabala Erenn (the Book of Invasions, compiled in the 11th century from older oral tradition), and they are the closest thing Irish myth has to a pantheon of gods. T2: they arrived in Ireland IN DARK CLOUDS -- so black that for three days the sun was hidden -- and LANDED ON THE MOUNTAINS in the west. The moment they stepped ashore, they BURNED THEIR OWN SHIPS behind them so that they would never think of retreating. The smoke of the ships was what darkened the sky (Lebor Gabala Erenn, redaction on the fifth invasion). T3: they came from FOUR CITIES in the north of the world -- FALIAS, GORIAS, FINDIAS, and MURIAS -- where they had learned poetry, wisdom, druid-magic, and the crafts of the smith. From each city they brought one of the FOUR TREASURES (see the four-treasures ladder). T4: their chief god is the DAGDA ('the good god', meaning good AT everything), their war-goddess is the MORRIGAN, their sun-god and master-of-all-arts is LUGH, their sea-god is MANANNAN MAC LIR, their patron of poetry and smithcraft is BRIGID, their god of love is AENGUS, their healer is DIAN CECHT, their first king is NUADA of the Silver Hand. T5: after the Tuatha De Danann were defeated by the sixth and last wave, the MILESIANS (the Gaels, the ancestors of the modern Irish), they did not die -- they RETREATED UNDERGROUND into the SIDHE (SHEE) mounds, the grassy hills scattered across Ireland. From that day they are called the AOS SI (the 'people of the mounds'), which becomes in English the FAIRY FOLK -- the Irish fairies of a thousand later stories are the Tuatha De Danann in retreat. Further rungs: the mother-goddess DANU (also called ANU) gave the people their name but appears in almost no surviving story -- she is a name behind a name; the DIVISION OF THE MOUNDS after the Milesian defeat was managed by MANANNAN MAC LIR, who gave each god a mound to live in (Aengus at Newgrange, the Dagda at Bru na Boinne, Midir at Bri Leith); the whole Book of Invasions with its six waves (Cessair, Partholon, Nemed, Fir Bolg, Tuatha De Danann, Milesians) is a medieval Irish attempt to fit native mythology into a Christian world-history frame, with Cessair as Noah's granddaughter escaping the Flood -- fascinating theological syncretism.
source: PRIMARY: Lebor Gabala Erenn (Book of Invasions, 11th c. compilation; on the fifth invasion -- Tuatha De arriving in dark clouds, burning ships, coming from four northern cities); Cath Maige Tuired (Second Battle of Moytura, 9-11th c. -- for gods named as characters); Acallam na Senorach (12th c., for the retreat into the sidhe mounds). SCHOLARLY: John Carey, A New Introduction to Lebor Gabala Erenn (1993); Marie-Louise Sjoestedt, Gods and Heroes of the Celts (1949); Proinsias Mac Cana, Celtic Mythology (1970); James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (1998). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Tuatha De Danann' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Tuatha De Danann', 'Lebor Gabala Erenn', 'Aos Si' -- god-people of Danu, arrival in dark clouds burning ships, four cities, retreat into sidhe mounds becoming the fairy folk. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact wording of Lebor Gabala on the dark clouds (recensions differ); which recension names Manannan as the one who divided the mounds (Altram Tige Da Medar is one source).
framing_note: FOUNDATIONAL Irish anchor -- must exist for every downstream ladder to reference 'the Tuatha De Danann'. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (they arrived in DARK CLOUDS and BURNED THEIR SHIPS the moment they landed so they could not retreat) and T5 (when they lost the last battle they DID NOT DIE -- they RETREATED UNDERGROUND into the fairy-mounds, and Ireland's fairy-folk are them). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the god-people who became the fairies' AND ask their name; describe the SCENE (a strange people arriving in unnatural dark clouds, burning their own ships on the beach, coming from four northern cities) and let the recall be the PEOPLE, the GODDESS whose name they carry, or the SHIPS. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Aesir arriving in Asgard, or the Olympians overthrowing the Titans, or Israel entering Canaan -- a founding-people myth in its own right, not glossed as 'primitive'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Irish invaders (Fir Bolg, Milesians, Fomorians -- all adjacent-real, own ladders), other Celtic goddess-names (BRIGID is inside the Tuatha; MACHA is one of the Morrigan; DANU is the mother-goddess; DONN is the god of the dead -- distinguish), other 'retreat underground' motifs (the Norse dwarves under the mountains -- other pillar). Wrong number of waves: SIX invasions in Lebor Gabala, not five, not seven.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns actual Irish archaeology (the pre-Celtic Neolithic peoples of Ireland, Iron-Age Celtic settlement); theology owns the MYTH of six-wave settlement in the Book of Invasions. GEOGRAPHY owns the physical sidhe mounds (Newgrange, Knowth, Dowth, the Hill of Tara) as places; theology owns who LIVES in them in story.

name: The Four Treasures: Lia Fail, Spear of Lugh, Sword of Nuada, Cauldron of the Dagda
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The four magical objects the Tuatha De Danann brought from their four northern cities, named individually and honestly. T1: when the Tuatha De Danann came to Ireland they brought FOUR TREASURES -- one from each of the FOUR CITIES they had studied in (FALIAS, GORIAS, FINDIAS, MURIAS). The four are so famous in Irish myth they are sometimes called simply 'the Hallows of Ireland' (Lebor Gabala Erenn; Cath Maige Tuired opening). T2: from FALIAS came the LIA FAIL, the STONE OF DESTINY. It was set on the HILL OF TARA -- the ancient seat of the High Kings of Ireland -- and it would CRY OUT WITH A LOUD SHRIEK beneath the feet of the man who was destined to be the rightful king of Ireland. When any true king stood on it, the stone screamed. When a pretender stood on it, silence. The Lia Fail is STILL ON THE HILL OF TARA today, a rough standing pillar about five feet tall. T3: from GORIAS came the SPEAR OF LUGH -- also called the GAI ASSAIL or SLEA BUA ('the victory spear'). No battle was ever lost in which it was carried, and NO CAST OF IT EVER MISSED. It burned red-hot from its own thirst and had to be QUENCHED IN A CAULDRON OF BLACK BLOOD or milk to be stilled between fights (see the Lugh ladder for how the spear kills Balor). T4: from FINDIAS came the SWORD OF NUADA -- the CLAIOMH SOLAIS, the 'SWORD OF LIGHT'. Once it was drawn from its sheath, NO ENEMY COULD ESCAPE IT and NO WOUND FROM IT COULD BE STAUNCHED. Nuada was the first king of the Tuatha De and this was his signature weapon (see the Nuada Silver-Hand ladder for the wound that cost him the throne). T5: from MURIAS came the CAULDRON OF THE DAGDA -- called the COIRE ANSIC ('the un-dry cauldron'). NO COMPANY EVER WENT AWAY FROM IT UNSATISFIED. Every warrior got as much as he needed, and the more you drew from it the more it held. It is the archetype behind every 'cauldron of plenty' in Celtic myth (and, some scholars argue, a distant ancestor of the Grail). Further rungs: the four cities are always listed FALIAS-GORIAS-FINDIAS-MURIAS and each teacher-name is preserved in medieval glosses (Morfessa in Falias, Esras in Gorias, Uiscias in Findias, Semias in Murias -- each an obscure druid-teacher); the Lia Fail crying under the rightful king survives as a MOTIF into the Scottish and English coronation-traditions -- a stone said to be the Lia Fail was taken to Scotland to become the Stone of Scone, then to England beneath the coronation-chair at Westminster (Scots and Irish scholars have disputed which stone is the 'real' Lia Fail for a thousand years); the four treasures map onto FOUR VIRTUES of kingship in the medieval Irish schools -- truth (Lia Fail), valour (spear), justice (sword), hospitality (cauldron).
source: PRIMARY: Lebor Gabala Erenn (Book of Invasions, 11th c. -- the four treasures listed with their cities and powers); Cath Maige Tuired opening paragraphs (Second Battle of Moytura, 9-11th c. -- same four listed as the Tuatha De's mythic dowry). Metrical Dindshenchas on the Lia Fail at Tara. SCHOLARLY: James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (1998); Proinsias Mac Cana, Celtic Mythology (1970). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Four Treasures of the Tuatha De Danann' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Four Treasures of the Tuatha De Danann', 'Lia Fail', 'Spear of Lugh', 'Claiomh Solais', 'Cauldron of the Dagda', 'Falias', 'Gorias', 'Findias', 'Murias' -- four cities, four treasures, each power. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: precise spelling of Claiomh Solais / Claidheamh Soluis (Old vs Modern Irish); whether the spear is Gai Assail or Areadbhar in the source in question.
framing_note: The FOUR-TREASURES ladder -- the wonder is the FOUR-BY-FOUR completeness (four cities, four objects, four powers). Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the STONE that SCREAMS under the rightful king, still standing on the Hill of Tara today) and T5 (the CAULDRON no one ever leaves hungry from). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'four magical objects' AND ask what they are; describe the SCENE (four northern cities of learning, four teachers, four treasures brought south) and let the recall be a SPECIFIC treasure, its CITY, or its POWER. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Norse dwarves' six treasures (Mjolnir, Gungnir, Draupnir, Skidbladnir, Gullinbursti, Sif's hair) or the Christian Instruments of the Passion or the Arthurian Round Table -- a founding-set of sacred objects. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Tuatha weapons (Manannan's sword Fragarach 'the Answerer' -- own ladder; the sling-stone of Lugh -- own ladder), other cauldrons (the cauldron of Bran the Blessed in Welsh myth -- adjacent-real from a different Celtic tradition; the Grail as later Christian refraction), other 'king-selecting stones' (the Sword in the Stone in Arthurian legend -- deliberate distractor from the SISTER pillar). Wrong pairings: the SPEAR is from GORIAS not Findias; the SWORD is from FINDIAS not Gorias -- kids will guess these swapped.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the HILL OF TARA as a place; theology owns what OBJECT still stands there. HISTORY owns the actual Stone of Scone / Coronation Chair at Westminster as a real coronation-object; theology owns the LEGEND that it is (or is not) the Lia Fail.

name: The Six Invasions of Ireland: from Cessair before the Flood to the Milesians
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The frame-narrative of Irish mythology -- how the whole Book of Invasions maps history. T1: the LEBOR GABALA ERENN, the 'Book of the Taking of Ireland' (compiled in the 11th century out of older material), tells that Ireland was settled in SIX WAVES, each wiping out or displacing the last. Kids can count them on one hand plus a thumb. T2: the FIRST wave was CESSAIR, granddaughter of NOAH, who came to Ireland to try to ESCAPE THE FLOOD -- fifty women and three men in a single ship; they landed forty days before the Flood, and all of them drowned except Cessair's husband FINTAN mac Bochra, who survived by turning into a SALMON. The SECOND was PARTHOLON, arriving three centuries after the Flood, whose people were wiped out by plague in a single week. The THIRD was NEMED, whose people fought the sea-raiding FOMORIANS and were reduced to thirty survivors. T3: the FOURTH wave was the FIR BOLG (the 'bag men' -- from a legend that they carried earth in leather bags as slaves in Greece before they escaped back to Ireland). They divided Ireland into the FIVE PROVINCES that survive to this day (Ulster, Leinster, Munster, Connacht, and the sacred middle province of MIDE -- Meath). T4: the FIFTH wave was the TUATHA DE DANANN, who arrived in dark clouds and DEFEATED the Fir Bolg at the FIRST BATTLE OF MOYTURA (Cath Maige Tuired Cunga) -- and then defeated their real enemies, the FOMORIANS, at the SECOND BATTLE OF MOYTURA. This is the wave of the GODS. T5: the SIXTH and FINAL wave was the MILESIANS -- the sons of MIL ESPAINE from Spain, the ancestors of the modern Irish Gaels. Their poet AMERGIN, stepping onto the shore, sang the AMERGIN GLUINGEL -- one of the oldest surviving poems in the Irish language -- 'I am a wind on the sea, I am a wave of the ocean, I am a stag of seven tines, I am a hawk on a cliff...' As the Milesians took the land, the Tuatha De Danann retreated underground into the sidhe mounds; the Milesians took the surface of Ireland, the Tuatha De took the underground. Every Irish person alive is descended (in the Book of Invasions frame) from the Milesians. Further rungs: FINTAN mac Bochra the salmon lives through all six invasions and can tell the whole story at the end (see the Fintan / Salmon of Knowledge overlap); the Book of Invasions is medieval SYNCRETISM -- a Christian monk trying to make Irish pagan cosmology fit inside a Genesis-and-Flood world-history; each wave has its own set of named characters (Cessair's fifty women each have a name in the manuscripts); AMERGIN's poem is one of the most-quoted early-Irish texts and every Celtic-revival writer from Yeats to Robert Graves has translated it.
source: PRIMARY: Lebor Gabala Erenn (Book of Invasions, 11th c. -- the six-wave frame, Cessair through Milesians, Fintan mac Bochra as the salmon survivor, Amergin's poem on landing). Multiple recensions (First, Second, Third Redaction) all preserve the six-wave frame. SCHOLARLY: John Carey, A New Introduction to Lebor Gabala Erenn (1993); R. A. Stewart Macalister edition and translation (Irish Texts Society, 5 vols. 1938-1956). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Lebor Gabala Erenn' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Lebor Gabala Erenn', 'Cessair', 'Partholon', 'Nemed', 'Fir Bolg', 'Milesians', 'Amergin Gluingel' -- six waves, each named, Fintan the salmon-survivor, Amergin's poem. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact number of Cessair's companions (50 women + 3 men in most sources); which recension gives the fullest Amergin text (Book of Leinster).
framing_note: The SIX-INVASIONS ladder -- the FRAME every other Irish ladder sits inside. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the FIRST wave was Noah's GRANDDAUGHTER trying to escape the Flood, and only her husband survived by turning into a SALMON) and T5 (the MILESIAN poet AMERGIN sang 'I AM A WIND ON THE SEA' as he stepped onto the shore). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem list the six waves AND ask which they are; describe the SCENE (a granddaughter of Noah trying to outrun the Flood, a poet singing on a beach, a Fifth wave arriving in dark clouds) and let the recall be a SPECIFIC wave-name, its LEADER, or its FATE. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell the Israelite conquest of Canaan, or the Greek generations from Titans to Olympians to heroes -- a founding-nation frame in a mythic key. DISTRACTOR MINE: the six waves themselves must be kept distinct (Cessair -- pre-Flood; Partholon -- plague; Nemed -- Fomorian raids; Fir Bolg -- bag-men + five provinces; Tuatha De -- the gods; Milesians -- the modern Irish), other flood-survivor stories (Noah himself -- OT; Deucalion in Greek -- adjacent from another pillar), other 'first poet on the beach' motifs. Wrong number: SIX waves, not five, not seven.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns actual Irish archaeology and pre-history; theology owns the MYTHIC six-wave frame the medieval Irish invented to sit alongside it. GEOGRAPHY owns the actual FIVE PROVINCES of Ireland (Ulster, Leinster, Munster, Connacht, Meath) as places; theology owns which mythic wave FOUNDED them.

name: Nuada Silver-Hand: the king who lost a throne with a hand
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The first king of the Tuatha De Danann in Ireland, and the wound that cost him his throne. T1: NUADA was the FIRST KING of the Tuatha De Danann in Ireland. He carried the SWORD OF LIGHT (Claiomh Solais) from Findias, one of the four treasures. He led his people to victory at the FIRST BATTLE OF MOYTURA against the Fir Bolg. T2: in that first battle, Nuada was wounded -- the Fir Bolg champion SRENG cut off his RIGHT HAND with one sword-stroke (Cath Maige Tuired Cunga, First Battle of Moytura). Nuada survived, but by the strict old Irish law of kingship, A KING MUST BE PHYSICALLY WHOLE -- a maimed man may not sit on the throne of Ireland. Nuada had to STEP DOWN. T3: the healer of the Tuatha De, DIAN CECHT, made Nuada a new hand out of SILVER, jointed so cleverly that every finger moved as freely as a real one. From that day Nuada is called NUADA AIRGETLAM -- NUADA OF THE SILVER HAND, or Nuada Silver-Arm. But a silver hand is still not a hand of flesh, so Nuada still could not be king. T4: while Nuada was healing, the Tuatha De chose BRES THE BEAUTIFUL to be king in his place -- a young man whose father was a FOMORIAN. Bres turned tyrant (see the Bres ladder), and the Tuatha De grew miserable under him. Meanwhile Dian Cecht's SON MIACH, a greater physician than his father, took Nuada's silver hand and REGREW A HAND OF LIVING FLESH in its place, joint by joint, over nine days and nights, singing 'sinew to sinew, nerve to nerve' (Cath Maige Tuired, sec 33). Nuada was whole again. T5: Dian Cecht, humiliated that his son had surpassed him, KILLED MIACH with four sword-strokes to the head. On Miach's grave grew THREE HUNDRED AND SIXTY-FIVE HERBS, one for every joint and nerve in the human body -- and Miach's sister AIRMED laid them out in order on her cloak to record their healing powers. But Dian Cecht came and OVERTURNED THE CLOAK, mixing the herbs beyond any hope of sorting -- and that (the story says) is why no human physician has ever known all the powers of all the herbs. Nuada, restored, was made king again and led the Tuatha De into the Second Battle of Moytura -- where he was killed by Balor's poison eye and the crown passed to Lugh. Further rungs: the story of Miach's regrown hand is preserved verbatim in Cath Maige Tuired sec 33, one of the tenderest passages in early Irish literature; the mixing-of-the-herbs on the cloak is a folk-etiology for why medicine is imperfect; DIAN CECHT is the ancestor of every named Irish healer-god or healer-saint in later tradition; NUADA is cognate with the Welsh NUDD and probably with the British god NODENS (a temple to Nodens survived at Lydney in Gloucestershire) -- the same god across three languages.
source: PRIMARY: Cath Maige Tuired Cunga (First Battle of Moytura, 12th c. text preserving older material -- Sreng cutting off Nuada's hand); Cath Maige Tuired (Second Battle of Moytura, 9-11th c. -- sec 11 Nuada's silver hand by Dian Cecht, sec 33 Miach regrowing flesh, killing of Miach, 365 herbs on the grave, Airmed and the cloak, mixing of the herbs). SCHOLARLY: Elizabeth Gray's edition and translation of Cath Maige Tuired (Irish Texts Society vol. 52, 1982); James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Nuada Airgetlam' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Nuada Airgetlam', 'Dian Cecht', 'Miach (mythology)', 'Airmed' -- hand cut off by Sreng, silver hand by Dian Cecht, disqualified from kingship, Miach regrows flesh hand, Dian Cecht kills Miach, 365 herbs on grave, Airmed's cloak. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact translation of the 'sinew to sinew, nerve to nerve' incantation (Whitley Stokes vs Elizabeth Gray).
framing_note: The NUADA anchor -- must exist for the Bres, Lugh, and Balor ladders to reference NUADA SILVER-HAND. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the KING had to STEP DOWN because he lost a HAND -- old Irish law said a king must be WHOLE) and T5 (the healer Dian Cecht KILLED HIS OWN SON out of jealousy and then MIXED UP 365 HEALING HERBS on the grave to spite him). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'silver-handed king' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a king wounded in battle, a physician crafting a hand of silver, a rule that no maimed man may rule) and let the recall be the KING, the METAL, or the RULE. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Tyr losing his hand to Fenrir, or Bran the Blessed's severed head speaking in Welsh myth, or Christ's wounds -- god-hero body-wounds as mythic weight. DISTRACTOR MINE: other one-handed / body-wound heroes (Tyr the Norse -- lost hand to Fenrir, adjacent pillar; Bran the Blessed -- Welsh; Fintan the salmon -- own ladder), other Tuatha De kings (Bres the tyrant -- own ladder; Lugh -- own ladder), other silver / metal body-parts (silver toes, gold beard). Wrong physician: MIACH is the son, DIAN CECHT is the jealous father -- MIACH heals with flesh, Dian Cecht made the silver.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY owns the abstract PRINCIPLE that rulers must be perfect / bodily whole; theology owns the Irish STORY of a king who lost his hand. HISTORY owns actual Iron-Age Celtic kingship customs; theology owns the mythic law encoded in the story.

name: Bres the Beautiful: the half-Fomorian tyrant
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: How the Tuatha De Danann tried a compromise king and got a tyrant, and how the world's first satire brought him down. T1: after NUADA lost his hand and stepped down from the throne (see that ladder), the Tuatha De Danann needed a new king. They chose BRES -- called BRES THE BEAUTIFUL because he was the handsomest man of his generation. His mother ERIU was a Tuatha De goddess; his father ELATHA was a FOMORIAN prince. Bres was a HALF-FOMORIAN, and this was meant to make peace with the Tuatha De's enemies (Cath Maige Tuired sec 24). T2: Bres turned out to be a terrible king. Under his rule the Fomorians began to IMPOSE HEAVY TRIBUTE on the Tuatha De -- so heavy that even the sons of gods had to work in menial labour. The Dagda himself was forced to DIG DITCHES like a common labourer, and Ogma, the god of eloquence, was forced to carry FIREWOOD like a slave (Cath Maige Tuired sec 25). T3: Bres was also MEAN. Old Irish kingship demanded HOSPITALITY -- a king must give food, drink, and gifts to any guest, and especially to poets. Bres would not. The poet CAIRPRE, son of Etain, came to Bres's hall and was housed in a tiny dark room, given three dry oatcakes and no meat and no beer (Cath Maige Tuired sec 39). T4: Cairpre left the next morning and, walking out onto the hillside, spoke a SATIRE against Bres -- the FIRST SATIRE EVER MADE IN IRELAND, the sources say. It is short enough to quote: 'WITHOUT FOOD SPEEDILY ON A DISH, / WITHOUT A COW'S MILK ON WHICH A CALF GROWS, / WITHOUT A MAN'S ABODE UNDER ITS ROOF AT NIGHT, / WITHOUT MEANS TO ENTERTAIN A BARDIC COMPANY -- / LET THAT BE BRES'S CONDITION' (Cath Maige Tuired sec 39, trans. Elizabeth Gray). T5: the moment the satire was spoken, RED BOILS BROKE OUT ON BRES'S FACE. In old Irish law a blemished king cannot rule (the same law that had put Nuada aside), so Bres was DEPOSED on the spot -- brought down by a POEM. Bres fled to his Fomorian father and returned with an army of Fomorians for the SECOND BATTLE OF MOYTURA, where Lugh would defeat him and Balor (see those ladders). Further rungs: the boils appear in Irish as 'THREE BOILS' -- one on Bres's cheek, one on his forehead, one on his brow -- so the blemish is unmistakable; CAIRPRE mac Etain becomes the archetype of the Irish satirist-poet whose word could kill or unking (the medieval Irish took satire so seriously that satirists had legal protection and rulers feared them); ERIU (Bres's mother) is one of the three eponymous goddess-queens of Ireland (Eriu, Banba, Fodla), from whose name comes EIRE (Ireland's Irish-language name).
source: PRIMARY: Cath Maige Tuired (Second Battle of Moytura, 9-11th c., Elizabeth Gray edition Irish Texts Society vol. 52, 1982 -- sec 24 Bres's parentage, sec 25 Dagda and Ogma reduced to labour, sec 39 Cairpre's satire verbatim, boils breaking out, Bres deposed). SCHOLARLY: John Carey; Elizabeth Gray's introduction; James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Bres' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Bres', 'Cath Maige Tuired', 'Cairbre mac Etaine' -- half-Fomorian king, tyranny, forcing gods into menial labour, insulting the poet Cairpre, first-ever satire, boils on face, deposed. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Elizabeth Gray's translation of the satire verbatim; whether the labouring god is Ogma or Ogmios in the passage.
framing_note: The BRES ladder -- the poet-brings-down-the-king story, one of the wonders of Irish myth. Dinner-test payoff: T4+T5 (a POET spoke a poem and RED BOILS appeared on the king's face and he lost the throne -- because Irish law said a BLEMISHED king could not rule; this was the FIRST SATIRE EVER MADE in Ireland). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'satire made the king lose his throne' AND ask who; describe the SCENE (a poet housed in a dark room with dry oatcakes, walking out at dawn to compose, a king waking with boils) and let the recall be the KING, the POET, or the BLEMISH. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Nathan the prophet confronting David, or the Greek chorus mocking a tyrant, or the medieval jester licensed to speak truth -- the ARTIST's word against the KING is a universal pattern, and the Irish gave it teeth. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Tuatha De kings (Nuada -- silver hand, own ladder; Lugh -- succeeds him, own ladder), other Fomorians (Balor, Elatha, Indech -- adjacent-real), other 'poet's-curse' motifs (Amergin's poem, Fintan's memory), other blemish-and-kingship stories (Nuada again). Wrong condition: NOT leprosy, NOT wounds -- BOILS specifically, the medieval Irish blemish of choice.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns actual Iron-Age Celtic legal traditions around kingship and satire; theology owns the Irish MYTH-EXEMPLAR of a poem deposing a king. PHILOSOPHY owns the reasoning move of 'legitimacy tied to bodily wholeness'; theology owns the specific story that dramatises it.

name: Lugh at Tara: the doorkeeper's list of arts
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: How the Ildanach, master of all arts, got into Tara -- one of the most famous scenes in all Irish literature. T1: LUGH was the greatest of the Tuatha De Danann -- part Tuatha De, part Fomorian, grandson of BALOR of the Evil Eye. He was called LUGH LAMHFHADA ('LONG-ARM' -- long enough to hurl the spear from Gorias any distance) and LUGH SAMILDANACH (SAM-IL-DA-NACH, meaning 'EQUALLY SKILLED IN ALL THE ARTS') and LUGH ILDANACH ('MASTER OF ALL ARTS'). T2: while Bres was still tyrannising the Tuatha De (see that ladder), Lugh grew to manhood in secret and came to TARA to offer himself in the fight against the Fomorians. He arrived at the gates of the royal hall wearing a golden fillet and asked to be let in. The DOORKEEPER (called CAMALL in some sources) stopped him and asked what SKILL he could offer, for 'no one enters Tara without an art no one else in the hall has' (Cath Maige Tuired sec 55). T3: Lugh said 'QUESTION ME -- I AM A WRIGHT (a carpenter).' The doorkeeper said, 'We have a wright already, Luchta.' Lugh said, 'I AM A SMITH.' 'We have Goibniu.' 'I AM A CHAMPION.' 'We have Ogma.' 'I AM A HARPER.' 'We have Abcan.' 'I AM A WARRIOR.' 'We have Bres and Breas.' 'I AM A POET AND HISTORIAN.' 'We have En mac Ethamain.' 'I AM A SORCERER.' 'We have druids and sorcerers.' 'I AM A PHYSICIAN.' 'We have Dian Cecht.' 'I AM A CUPBEARER.' 'We have nine.' 'I AM A CRAFTSMAN IN BRASS.' 'We have Credne.' T4: Lugh let each refusal land. Then he asked the killing question: 'BUT HAVE YOU ONE MAN WHO IS ALL OF THESE AT ONCE?' The doorkeeper had no answer, and had to run inside to tell King Nuada, who ordered the gate opened. This is the origin of Lugh's title SAMILDANACH -- because he could do ALL those crafts at ONCE. T5: inside Nuada's hall Lugh proved every claim -- he played the SLEEPING STRAIN, the WEEPING STRAIN, and the LAUGHING STRAIN on the harp (see the Dagda's harp ladder for the same three strains); he threw a great stone that only three-quarters of a hundred men could lift; he beat Nuada himself at FIDCHELL (the Irish board-game). Nuada gave up his own throne and let Lugh sit in it for THIRTEEN DAYS to prepare for the Second Battle of Moytura -- because 'it was easier that a king should stand for a champion than that a champion stand for a king' (Cath Maige Tuired sec 74). It is Lugh who then leads the Tuatha De to victory at Moytura and kills his own grandfather Balor. Further rungs: the doorkeeper scene at Tara (Cath Maige Tuired sec 55) is a set-piece Irish schoolchildren still learn; the LIST of arts (wright, smith, champion, harper, warrior, poet, historian, sorcerer, physician, cupbearer, craftsman) is one of the most complete inventories of high-status skills in the ancient Irish world; LUGH gave his name to the medieval-Irish harvest festival LUGHNASADH ('Lugh's assembly'), which survives in Ireland as the August bank-holiday Lughnasa; the Roman-conquest historians identified Lugh with MERCURY as 'the god the Gauls most worship, and to whom they set up the most images' (Julius Caesar, Gallic Wars 6.17).

name: Balor of the Evil Eye and the eyelid four men had to lift
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The great Fomorian king whose gaze slew armies, and the grandson-prophecy that killed him. T1: the FOMORIANS were the ancient sea-monster-people of Irish myth, the enemies of every wave of settlers before the Tuatha De Danann -- misshapen, one-legged, one-eyed, and cruel. Their king at the time of the Second Battle of Moytura was BALOR of the EVIL EYE (BALOR NA SUILE NIMHE), and Balor was the most terrible being in Irish mythology. T2: Balor had ONE EYE, and it was so poisonous that whatever it LOOKED AT DIED. The eye had grown so venomous from Balor's father's poisonous druid-fumes as a boy that the eyelid had grown thick and heavy, and Balor could NOT LIFT IT ALONE. FOUR WARRIORS with HOOKS AND ROPES had to haul the eyelid up whenever Balor needed to see -- and once the eye was open, ENTIRE ARMIES fell dead where they stood (Cath Maige Tuired sec 133 and later Donegal folk-tradition). T3: Balor had also heard a prophecy: he would be KILLED by his OWN GRANDSON. He had one daughter, ETHLINN (or Eithne), and to prevent her from ever bearing a child he locked her in a CRYSTAL TOWER on TORY ISLAND, off the coast of Donegal, with twelve women as her only company and no man ever to be admitted. T4: CIAN of the Tuatha De -- son of Dian Cecht -- came in disguise to the tower (in some versions with the help of a druidess called BIROG), was let in, and lay with Ethlinn. She bore TRIPLETS. Balor found out, took the three babies, wrapped them in a sheet, and had them thrown into the SEA to drown. Two drowned, but ONE -- LUGH -- was caught on the water by a wave, or was rescued by MANANNAN MAC LIR the sea-god, and was carried away to be fostered in secret. T5: at the SECOND BATTLE OF MOYTURA, Balor and Lugh met on the battlefield -- grandfather and grandson. The four men lifted Balor's eyelid, and the eye began to open toward the Tuatha De ranks. Before the eye was fully open, LUGH cast a SLING-STONE (or in some versions a SPEAR of the FOUR TREASURES, from Gorias) with his LONG ARM. The stone struck Balor square in the open eye, drove clean through his skull, and burst out the BACK OF HIS HEAD -- turning the poisonous gaze BACKWARDS onto Balor's OWN army, killing the Fomorian ranks behind him with their own king's eye. The prophecy was fulfilled and the Fomorians were broken forever (Cath Maige Tuired sec 133-135). Further rungs: the eye-through-the-head detail is preserved in FOLKLORE from Donegal all the way into the 19th c. -- the local story is still told at MIZEN HEAD and TORY ISLAND today; BIROG the druidess is one of the few named female druids in Irish myth; the sling-stone Lugh used is called by some sources TATHLUM ('concrete-ball') and was made of the brains of enemies mixed with lime (a gruesome detail preserved in a 15th-c. text); the parallel to the Perseus / Acrisius grandfather-prophecy (a grandfather locks a daughter away to prevent a grandson, is killed by that grandson anyway) is a striking Indo-European motif shared with Greek myth.

Irish Texts Society vol. 52, 1982 -- sec 133-135 the killing of Balor, sling-stone through eye, gaze turned back). Dinner-test payoff: T2 (his ONE eye was so heavy with poison that FOUR MEN with HOOKS AND ROPES had to lift the eyelid, and once opened it KILLED AN ARMY where they stood) and T5 (his GRANDSON killed him with a SLING-STONE straight through the eye and out the back -- and the poison gaze then killed BALOR'S OWN ARMY behind him). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Perseus killing his grandfather Acrisius (the Greek grandfather-prophecy parallel) or the Cyclops Polyphemus blinded by Odysseus -- the one-eyed monster king, a universal pattern. DISTRACTOR MINE: other one-eyed figures (Odin the Norse -- adjacent pillar; Polyphemus the Cyclops -- Greek pillar; Horus's eye -- non-Western, out of scope), other prophesied grandfathers (Acrisius killed by Perseus -- exact Greek parallel, deliberately-adjacent trap), other Fomorians (Bres the half-Fomorian, Elatha, Indech -- own ladders). Wrong number: FOUR men lifting the eyelid, not two, not three, not eight.

name: The Dagda: his club, his harp, his cauldron
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The 'good god' of the Tuatha De Danann and his three signature possessions. T1: the DAGDA (pronounced DAG-da) is the CHIEF of the Tuatha De Danann. His name doesn't mean 'good' morally -- it means 'GOOD AT EVERYTHING'. He is called EOCHAID OLLATHAIR ('the All-Father'), RUAD RO-FHESSA ('the Lord of Great Knowledge'), and simply THE DAGDA. He is depicted as huge, coarse, red-bearded, and full-bellied -- and formidable in every craft. T2: he carries a great CLUB, called the LORG MOR ('the great staff'), so heavy that eight men could not lift it and it had to be dragged on wheels leaving a ditch behind it in the earth. The club had TWO ENDS: one end KILLED ANY MAN it struck DEAD ON THE SPOT, and the OTHER END BROUGHT THE DEAD BACK TO LIFE. Life and death, one weapon (Book of Leinster, Sanas Cormaic). T3: he owned a magic HARP called UAITHNE, made of dark oak, that would answer only to the Dagda's voice. When the Fomorians stole it after the Second Battle of Moytura, the Dagda came into their feast-hall, spoke the harp's two secret bynames, and it flew off the wall to his hand, killing NINE FOMORIANS in its flight (Cath Maige Tuired sec 162). The harp could play THREE STRAINS: the GOLTRAI (the WEEPING STRAIN, at which no one who heard it could keep from crying), the GEANTRAI (the LAUGHING STRAIN, at which no one could keep from laughing), and the SUANTRAI (the SLEEPING STRAIN, at which everyone in the hall fell into a deep sleep). T4: he owned the CAULDRON OF PLENTY, the COIRE ANSIC ('the un-dry cauldron'), one of the four treasures brought from the city of MURIAS (see the four-treasures ladder). NO ASSEMBLY WENT AWAY UNSATISFIED from it -- every warrior got as much as his hunger called for, and the more you took the more it held. T5: for all his majesty, the stories of the Dagda have a broad HUMOR to them. In Cath Maige Tuired sec 89-93 the Fomorians serve him a truce-meal of PORRIDGE: 80 gallons of milk plus flour plus fat plus a whole HERD of sheep, pigs, and goats, boiled all together in a hole in the ground. They give him a spoon so big 'a man and a woman could lie in it.' The Dagda EATS THE WHOLE LOT (the Fomorians thought no man could) and then walks off with a belly 'bigger than the greatest cauldron in a great household', dragging his club and leaving a ditch. He then makes a wooing arrangement with the daughter of the Fomorian king Indech -- a wonderfully rude story kept intact by the monk-copyists. Further rungs: the Dagda's tryst with the MORRIGAN at the ford at SAMHAIN before the Second Battle of Moytura (see the Morrigan ladder); the Dagda's dwelling is BRU NA BOINNE (the Newgrange complex) until his son AENGUS tricks him out of it (see the Aengus ladder); the harp's two secret bynames are given in Cath Maige Tuired -- DAUR DA BLA ('Oak of Two Meadows') and COIR CETHARCHAIR ('Four-Angled Music'); the three strains of music are a lasting frame in Irish tradition and appear again in the Fionn cycle attached to the Dagda's harper AUGHAIRE.

Irish Texts Society vol. 52, 1982 -- sec 89-93 the porridge scene, sec 162 the retrieval of the harp Uaithne, three strains). Sanas Cormaic ('Cormac's Glossary', 9th c.) on the Dagda's club. Book of Leinster on the Coire Ansic. SCHOLARLY: James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology; John Carey; Marie-Louise Sjoestedt, Gods and Heroes of the Celts. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'The Dagda' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'The Dagda', 'Uaithne', 'Coire Ansic', 'Lorg Mor', 'Cath Maige Tuired' -- club with two ends, harp Uaithne with two bynames and three strains (weeping/laughter/sleep), cauldron of plenty from Murias, porridge scene, huge-bellied. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Cath Maige Tuired sec 162 kills nine Fomorians in the harp's flight (recensions vary on the number); exact translation of the harp's two secret bynames.
framing_note: The DAGDA anchor -- must exist for the Morrigan-at-the-ford, Aengus-at-Newgrange, and Brigid ladders to reference their father. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (his CLUB kills with one end and BRINGS THE DEAD BACK with the other) and T3 (his HARP played the WEEPING, LAUGHING, and SLEEPING STRAINS -- no listener could hold back from crying, laughing, or falling asleep). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the good god' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a huge red-bearded god dragging a wheeled club, a harp on a hall wall, a bottomless cauldron) and let the recall be the GOD, the OBJECT, or the SPECIFIC POWER. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Odin's spear-and-ring set, or Thor's hammer-and-goats -- a chief-god with signature objects. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Tuatha De weapons (Nuada's Claiomh Solais -- own ladder; Lugh's spear -- own ladder; Manannan's Fragarach -- own ladder), other magic musical instruments (Apollo's lyre; Orpheus's lyre -- Greek pillar), other cauldrons (the cauldron of Bran in Welsh; the cauldron of Ceridwen). Wrong strain: the harp plays THREE strains (WEEPING, LAUGHING, SLEEPING), not four, not two.

HISTORY owns the actual Iron-Age Celtic feast-and-cauldron culture; theology owns the mythic bottomless cauldron that dramatises it.

name: The Morrigan at the ford: crow, prophecy, tryst
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The war-goddess of the Tuatha De Danann, her three names, and her tryst with the Dagda before Moytura. T1: the MORRIGAN (MOR-REE-GAN, meaning 'the GREAT QUEEN' or 'the PHANTOM QUEEN') is the war-and-prophecy goddess of the Tuatha De Danann. She appears at BATTLES in the shape of a CROW -- black-winged, sitting on shield-rims and spear-points, screaming over the slaughter. Whichever side she sits on, they are the ones about to die. T2: she is a THREE-IN-ONE goddess. Her three aspects (or three sisters, depending on the recension) are named BADB ('the Scald-Crow', battle-hag), MACHA (patron of horses and the goddess whose name is on Emain Macha and Armagh), and NEMAIN ('Frenzy') -- or in some texts the third sister is ANAND. Together the three are simply 'THE MORRIGAN'. T3: before the Second Battle of Moytura, the Dagda came to a FORD on the RIVER UNIUS in what is now County Sligo. He found the Morrigan there, one foot on the north bank and one foot on the south, WASHING at the water. She was ASTRIDE the ford at SAMHAIN (November 1, the old Irish new year, when the barrier between worlds is thinnest). The Dagda LAY WITH HER AT THE FORD, and in return she pledged to help the Tuatha De -- 'to draw the blood from the heart of the Fomorian king INDECH', to summon Ireland's magicians, and to break the Fomorian will (Cath Maige Tuired sec 84). T4: another face of the Morrigan is the WASHER AT THE FORD -- a woman met beside a stream, washing bloody armor in the water. She never speaks first. When you ask whose armor she is washing, she answers with YOUR NAME. To meet the Washer at the Ford is a death-omen; Cuchulainn met her (see the Cuchulainn ladder) and knew he would die that day. This is the origin of the later Irish and Scottish figure of the BEAN-SIDHE / BANSHEE, the wailing woman who warns of death. T5: at Moytura the Morrigan sat on a black-thorn stake above the battlefield, screaming the Tuatha De into fury and the Fomorians into panic. After Balor was dead and the Fomorians were broken, she stood on the mountain and PROPHESIED THE END OF THE WORLD -- a long dark poem preserved in Cath Maige Tuired sec 166-167: 'Summer without flowers, cattle without milk, women without shame, men without valour... crimes shall be praised, evil shall be honoured...' It is one of the earliest ragnarok-style prophecies in Western literature. Further rungs: the Morrigan's tryst with the Dagda at the ford is a SACRED-MARRIAGE motif (the god of the tribe unites with the goddess of the land to secure victory) that survives across Indo-European myth; the CROW as a Morrigan-form is the reason ravens and crows on Irish battlefields were always read as omens of death; the phrase 'THREE MORRIGNA' is preserved in the Metrical Dindshenchas as an old formulaic name; the Morrigan is the model for later figures from Shakespeare's WEIRD SISTERS in Macbeth (via the Scottish Bean-Sidhe) to the Battle-Crow of countless later British and Irish poetry.

Irish Texts Society vol. 52, 1982 -- sec 84 the tryst at the ford at Samhain, sec 166-167 the end-of-the-world prophecy). Tain Bo Cuailnge (Book of Leinster and Ulster Cycle -- Morrigan as crow on Cuchulainn's shoulder, Washer at the Ford). Metrical Dindshenchas (place-name traditions for Odras / Odras's Pond where the Morrigan drowned a herdswoman). SCHOLARLY: Rosalind Clark, The Great Queens: Irish Goddesses from the Morrigan to Cathleen ni Houlihan (1991); Angelique Gulermovich Epstein, War Goddess: The Morrigan and Her Germano-Celtic Counterparts (1998); James MacKillop. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a goddess ASTRIDE the ford at SAMHAIN, one foot on each bank, waiting for the chief-god who would lie with her to seal a war-alliance) and T4 (the WASHER AT THE FORD -- a woman met washing bloody armor in a stream, and if you ask her whose armor it is she names YOU). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'crow-goddess of war' AND ask her name; describe the SCENE (a black-winged bird settling on a shield-rim before battle, a woman astride a ford at Samhain, a washer at a stream with bloody armor) and let the recall be the GODDESS, the RIVER, or the WASHER-motif. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Norns weaving Norse fate, or Athena appearing on the battlefield at Troy, or the Angel of Death passing over Egypt -- a fate-and-battle figure across pillars. DISTRACTOR MINE: other three-in-one goddesses (the Greek Fates / Moirai -- Clotho / Lachesis / Atropos; the Norse Norns -- Urd / Verdandi / Skuld; adjacent-real from other pillars), other war-goddesses (Athena, Enyo, the Valkyries), other 'washer at the water' motifs (the Bean-Sidhe / Banshee descendant -- Irish folklore; Undine / Melusine -- French romance). Wrong tryst-partner: the Morrigan's ford-tryst is with the DAGDA specifically, not with Lugh, not with Nuada.

HISTORY / literature owns Shakespeare's Weird Sisters in Macbeth; theology owns the Irish MORRIGAN who is their remote ancestor via the banshee tradition.

name: Brigid of the Tuatha: poetry, healing, smithcraft, the sacred fire
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The Tuatha De goddess of the three crafts, and the astonishing survival of her cult under a saint's name. T1: BRIGID (BRIG-id or BREE-id) is a daughter of the DAGDA and one of the most important goddesses of the Tuatha De Danann. Her name is thought to mean 'the EXALTED ONE'. She is the patron of THREE crafts: POETRY (which was the highest-status Irish craft), HEALING, and SMITHCRAFT (the making of weapons at the forge) -- so she is called BRIGID OF THE POETS, BRIGID OF THE HEALERS, and BRIGID OF THE SMITHS. T2: she is (in Sanas Cormaic, 'Cormac's Glossary', 9th c.) 'a goddess whom poets worshipped, for very great and very famous was her protecting care' -- and she is described as having TWO SISTERS, also named Brigid, one the healer and one the smith -- so 'the three Brigids' are again a three-in-one goddess (a shape Irish gods take often, see the Morrigan). T3: her sacred symbol is FIRE -- specifically a PERPETUAL FLAME kept burning day and night by nineteen priestesses on a rotation, one for each day of a twenty-day cycle (the twentieth day the goddess herself was said to tend it). The flame was kept at KILDARE (CILL DARA, 'church of the oak') in Leinster. T4: when Ireland converted to Christianity in the 5th-6th centuries, the cult of the goddess did not die -- it was ABSORBED. A Christian ST. BRIGID OF KILDARE (c. 451-525) is founded on the same site, in the same shrine, tending the SAME PERPETUAL FLAME with the SAME nineteen nuns on the same rotation. The transformation is so seamless that most scholars now accept the saint's cult grew directly out of the goddess's cult -- the pagan flame kept burning under a Christian name for a thousand years. The flame was extinguished only in 1220 (by an English archbishop who thought it too pagan) and RE-LIT in 1993 by the Brigidine Sisters of Kildare, where it still burns. T5: the goddess Brigid also owns the festival of IMBOLC (February 1) -- the beginning of spring in the old Irish calendar, when the ewes begin to give milk. Imbolc becomes ST. BRIGID'S DAY in the Christian calendar. On the eve of Imbolc, Irish farm-families make a BRIGID'S CROSS out of woven rushes -- a four-armed cross with a woven square in the middle -- and hang it over the threshold of the house to bring protection and blessing for the coming year. Kids in Ireland still make them in school today, one thousand five hundred years after the goddess's name went underground. Further rungs: the Brigid-of-the-forge aspect gives her a cognate in the Roman MINERVA and the British MINERVA-SULIS at Bath (goddess of a hot spring, patron of the healing waters); the OAK at Cill Dara is the sacred tree of the site, echoing the Druids' well-known reverence for oaks; the ORDINATION of St. Brigid as a BISHOP in her early biography (the Bethu Brigte, 9th c.) is a scandal to some medievalists and a curiosity to others -- it may reflect the goddess-priestess authority absorbed into the saint; the CROSS OF BRIGID is not a Christian shape at all -- it is a SUN-WHEEL / EQUAL-ARM design older than Christianity in Ireland.

Bethu Brigte ('The Life of Brigid', 9th c. Irish life) and Cogitosus, Vita Brigitae (c. 650, earliest Latin life -- perpetual fire tended by nineteen nuns at Kildare, no fire tenders male, ordination as bishop). SCHOLARLY: Sean O Duinn, The Rites of Brigid, Goddess and Saint (2004); Miranda Green, Celtic Goddesses (1995); Lisa Bitel, Landscape with Two Saints: How Genovefa of Paris and Brigit of Kildare Built Christianity in Barbarian Europe (2009). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Brigid' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Brigid', 'Brigid of Kildare', 'Imbolc', 'St Brigid's cross', 'Perpetual fire of Brigid' -- goddess of poetry/healing/smithcraft, three sisters, perpetual flame at Kildare, nineteen nuns, extinguished 1220 re-lit 1993, Imbolc = St Brigid's Day February 1, woven-rush cross. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: nineteen vs twenty priestesses (Cogitosus vs later sources); Bethu Brigte on the bishop-ordination scene.
framing_note: The BRIGID ladder -- the most fascinating case in Irish myth of goddess-into-saint continuity. Dinner-test payoff: T3+T4 (a PERPETUAL FLAME at KILDARE tended in rotation by NINETEEN priestesses, then by NINETEEN NUNS after the conversion -- the SAME FLAME on the SAME SITE, burning from the pagan cult straight into the Christian one until an archbishop put it out in 1220, and it was RE-LIT in 1993) and T5 (Irish kids still weave BRIGID'S CROSSES from rushes every February 1, in a rite older than Ireland's Christianity). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'goddess of the perpetual flame' AND ask her name; describe the SCENE (a fire tended by nineteen women on rotation, a woven-rush cross hung on a threshold, a goddess of three crafts) and let the recall be BRIGID, the SITE (Kildare), or the NUMBER of tenders. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: this ladder is where the Kids Bank's ALL-FOUR-PILLARS-ON-THE-SAME-PLANE rule is easiest to see -- the goddess-into-saint TRANSITION is presented as fascinating cultural history, not as evidence for or against either tradition's truth-claim. Told the way one would tell the Roman VESTAL VIRGINS tending their perpetual flame at the temple of Vesta -- a matched pagan-and-then-Christian keeping-of-fire. NO smug-atheist 'the Christians appropriated' framing; NO smug-believer 'the goddess prefigured the saint' framing -- just the historical continuity. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Tuatha De goddesses (the Morrigan, Danu, Boann, Airmed -- adjacent-real, own ladders), other fire-keeping cults (Vesta and the Vestal Virgins in Rome -- adjacent-real, other pillar), other saints often confused (Bridget of Sweden -- 14th c., completely different figure). Wrong number: NINETEEN priestesses/nuns, not twelve, not seven.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual medieval Kildare monastery (founded c. 480 by St. Brigid) and its full monastic history; theology owns the LEGEND of the perpetual fire and its goddess-continuity. GEOGRAPHY owns KILDARE as a place; theology owns why it matters -- the OAK and the FIRE. Sister-bank overlap: goddess-into-saint continuity is a moral-vision-flag topic because both directions of interpretation (Christian celebration; smug-atheist dismissal) must be resisted.

name: Manannan mac Lir: the Wave-Sweeper, Enbarr, and Emain Ablach
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The sea-god of the Tuatha De Danann and his three most famous possessions. T1: MANANNAN MAC LIR (MAN-a-nawn mac LEER) is the SEA-GOD of the Tuatha De Danann. His name means 'MANANNAN son of the SEA'. He rules the western sea and the OTHERWORLDLY ISLANDS west of Ireland, and he wears a CLOAK OF MIST (fetu fiada) that can hide him or make anyone he covers invisible. T2: he owns a BOAT called the SGUABA TUINNE ('WAVE-SWEEPER'). It has NO OARS and NO SAILS and needs NO WIND -- it simply KNOWS where you want to go and takes you there across the sea (Book of Leinster; Oidheadh Chloinne Tuireann, 'The Fate of the Children of Tuireann'). It later becomes the boat that carries Lugh across the sea to Ireland when he is an infant escaping Balor. T3: he owns a HORSE called ENBARR (Aonbharr, 'the One-Mane') that can gallop over LAND AND OVER THE SEA equally well -- his hooves strike the water and do not sink. Enbarr is later borrowed by Lugh to ride into the Second Battle of Moytura. T4: Manannan owns the SWORD FRAGARACH ('THE ANSWERER'). No armor can turn its blade aside; anyone struck by it must ANSWER any question put to them, and cannot lie under its point. He gave it eventually to Lugh, and Lugh passed it on into the Cuchulainn cycle -- a weapon that walks across the whole of Irish mythology. T5: Manannan rules a chain of PARADISE ISLANDS west of Ireland -- EMAIN ABLACH ('the ISLE OF APPLES', where the trees are always in fruit and no one grows old), MAG MELL ('the PLAIN OF DELIGHTS'), and TIR TAIRNGIRE ('the LAND OF PROMISE'). It is Manannan who ferries the souls of dead heroes westward across the sea to Emain Ablach -- a role that parallels the Greek Elysium and (astonishingly) the Arthurian AVALON ('Insula Avallonis', the ISLE OF APPLES), which owes its name and probably its whole picture to Emain Ablach. When the Milesians defeated the Tuatha De, it was Manannan who led the surviving gods into the SIDHE MOUNDS and gave each god one, and it was Manannan who fed them the FEAST OF GOIBNIU (an eternal feast that keeps the gods young). Further rungs: the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea is TRADITIONALLY named for Manannan -- 'Manannan's land', Ellan Vannin in Manx; the Manx flag's three-legged triskelion is sometimes read as his three-legged mount; the whole GENRE of Irish 'IMMRAM' voyage-tales (Voyage of Bran son of Febal, Voyage of Mael Duin) is Manannan's stories -- kids sailing west and finding wonder-islands; Manannan is one of the few Irish gods who appears both in Irish AND in Welsh myth (as Manawydan fab Llyr in the Mabinogion); Fragarach the Answerer eventually appears in the possession of Conn of the Hundred Battles, tying Manannan to the mortal high-king lists.
source: PRIMARY: Oidheadh Chloinne Tuireann ('The Fate of the Children of Tuireann', likely 14-15th c. compilation of older material -- Wave-Sweeper, Enbarr, Fragarach as Lugh's inheritance from Manannan). Book of Leinster. Immram Brain maic Febail ('The Voyage of Bran son of Febal', 7-8th c.) and Echtra Cormaic ('The Adventure of Cormac in the Land of Promise'). Metrical Dindshenchas. SCHOLARLY: Charles W. MacQuarrie, The Biography of the Irish God of the Sea from The Voyage of Bran (2004); James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology; John Carey. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (a BOAT with NO OARS, NO SAILS, and NO NEED OF WIND -- it just KNOWS where you want to go) and T5 (his ISLE OF APPLES west of Ireland -- EMAIN ABLACH -- is almost certainly the source of the Arthurian AVALON, which also means 'Isle of Apples'). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Poseidon with his trident and horses, or Njord and the Vanir sea-gods, or Christ walking on water -- the sea-god pattern across pillars. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Tuatha De artifacts (Wave-Sweeper is Manannan's, Enbarr is Manannan's, Fragarach is Manannan's-then-Lugh's -- keep them straight from the FOUR TREASURES from the four cities, own ladder), other sea-gods (Poseidon, Njord, Aegir the Norse -- adjacent from other pillars), other paradise-islands (Avalon in Arthurian -- direct cousin; the Greek Isles of the Blessed; the Norse Hel and Valhalla; Tir na nOg -- own Oisin ladder). Wrong island-name: EMAIN ABLACH, not Tir na nOg (which is a separate Isle of Eternal Youth from the Oisin cycle).

Sister-pillar overlap: EMAIN ABLACH and AVALON are almost certainly the same island under different tradition-names -- the Arthurian pillar owns Avalon per se; the Irish pillar owns Emain Ablach and the naming-cousin observation.

name: Aengus and the Dream: the swan-maiden of Loch Bel Dracon
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The love-god of the Tuatha De and his three-year search for a girl he had only seen in a dream, from Aislinge Oenguso ('The Dream of Aengus', 8-9th c.). T1: AENGUS (also spelled OENGUS, and called AENGUS OG -- 'YOUNG AENGUS' -- to mark him as the LOVE-GOD of the Tuatha De) is the son of the DAGDA and the river-goddess BOANN. He lives at BRU NA BOINNE (the Newgrange complex, on the River Boyne). Four birds are always seen flying around his head -- said to be his kisses turned to birds. T2: one night Aengus, still a young man, dreamed of the most beautiful woman he had ever seen standing at the foot of his bed. When he reached for her, she vanished. She came again every night for a YEAR, and every night vanished. Aengus fell so sick with love that he could not eat and would not speak. T3: his mother BOANN searched every hill and glen of Ireland for a year, looking for the woman of the dream. She could not find her. His father the DAGDA searched for another year. No luck. Finally the king of the Munster sidhe, BODB DERG, searched for a THIRD year, and found her -- at LOCH BEL DRACON ('the LAKE OF THE DRAGON'S MOUTH'), among a company of ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY WOMEN, chained in pairs by silver chains, with GOLD CHAINS ONLY around the neck of the fairest -- the woman of the dream. Her name was CAER IBORMEITH ('YEW-BERRY'), daughter of ETHAL Anbual. T4: the trouble was, Caer was a SWAN-MAIDEN. Every SAMHAIN (November 1) she and her hundred-and-fifty companions turned into SWANS for a full year, then back into girls on the next Samhain, then back into swans the year after. When Aengus came to the lake on Samhain morning, Caer and the hundred-and-fifty were on the water as swans. Aengus called out to her; Caer said she would only come to him if HE COULD BECOME A SWAN TOO. So Aengus turned himself into a swan, joined her on the water, and the two of them flew away together -- circling Bru na Boinne three times, singing music so sweet that everyone in Ireland who heard it FELL ASLEEP FOR THREE DAYS AND THREE NIGHTS (Aislinge Oenguso, closing scene). T5: Aengus's home BRU NA BOINNE (which is the modern NEWGRANGE, older than the Egyptian pyramids by 500 years) originally belonged to his FATHER the Dagda. Aengus TRICKED the Dagda out of it -- he asked for the Bru 'for a day and a night', and when the day and night were up Aengus said 'well, all of time is just a series of days and nights' and held the Bru forever after. The trick is preserved in the Tochmarc Etaine and the Metrical Dindshenchas. Further rungs: Aengus's four kiss-birds are the origin of a whole strand of Irish poetry about love-as-birds; the SWAN-couple motif in Irish myth (Aengus and Caer, the Children of Lir, Cuchulainn's Fand) is one of the most recurrent images in the whole tradition; Caer's name IBORMEITH means 'YEW-BERRY' -- the yew being the Irish tree of eternity because it grew in graveyards and lived forever; the Aengus-tricks-Dagda-out-of-Bru story is the origin of the great Irish trope of the CLEVER YOUNG SON outwitting the OLD FATHER for his inheritance.
source: PRIMARY: Aislinge Oenguso ('The Dream of Aengus', 8-9th c. Irish tale, ed. Francis Shaw 1934; also in Book of the Dun Cow). Tochmarc Etaine ('The Wooing of Etain', 12th c. compilation of older tales -- Aengus tricking the Dagda out of Bru na Boinne, 'a day and a night'). Metrical Dindshenchas on Bru na Boinne. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Aengus' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Aengus', 'Aislinge Oenguso', 'Caer Ibormeith', 'Boann' -- love-god son of Dagda and Boann, dream every night for a year, three-year search by Boann Dagda Bodb Derg, Caer at Loch Bel Dracon with 150 companions, gold chains vs silver, Samhain swan-transformation, Aengus becomes swan, three-days-of-sleep music, tricks Dagda out of Bru na Boinne. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (three parents searched THREE YEARS running -- mother, father, then a king -- for a girl the young god had only seen in a DREAM) and T4 (the girl was a SWAN-MAIDEN who spent every other year as a swan, and he had to BECOME A SWAN HIMSELF to be with her; their music put all Ireland to sleep for three days). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'young love-god with the swan-maiden' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a young god sick from a nightly dream, a lake full of chained swan-women, a swan-couple flying and singing) and let the recall be AENGUS, the SWAN-MAIDEN's name Caer, or the LOCH. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Cupid and Psyche, or Orpheus and Eurydice, or Beren and Luthien (Tolkien's homage to the Irish material) -- a mythic love-quest across worlds. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Irish swan-transformations (the CHILDREN OF LIR turned to swans for 900 years -- adjacent-real, own ladder; Cuchulainn's love Fand -- adjacent), other 'love-sick-from-a-dream' motifs (Midir and Etain -- own ladder from same manuscript), other Aengus stories (tricking the Dagda out of Bru). Wrong lake: LOCH BEL DRACON specifically, not Loch Neagh, not Loch Derg.

LITERATURE owns W.B. Yeats's poem 'The Song of Wandering Aengus'; theology owns the myth Yeats was retelling.

name: Midir and Etain: a fly, a hundred years, a game of fidchell
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The Wooing of Etain -- one of the most intricate Irish myths, from Tochmarc Etaine (10-12th c. compilation). T1: MIDIR (MEE-dir) is a Tuatha De god who lives in the sidhe mound of BRI LEITH in the modern County Longford. He falls in love with a beautiful woman named ETAIN and marries her; she is the most beautiful woman ever born in Ireland (Tochmarc Etaine part I). T2: Midir already had a WIFE, FUAMNACH, who was a POWERFUL DRUIDESS. When Midir brought Etain home, Fuamnach was so jealous that she TURNED ETAIN into a POOL OF WATER -- the water evaporated -- Etain rose from the vapour as a beautiful PURPLE FLY (in some translations, a butterfly). Even as a fly, she was so beautiful that her wing-buzz was sweet music and her scent healed the sick. T3: Fuamnach was not done. She raised a WIND that blew the fly for SEVEN YEARS through the sky, up and down all Ireland, never settling. The fly finally landed in the CUP of a Tuatha De hostess called ETAR, who drank her down without noticing. Nine months later Etar gave birth to a baby girl who was REBORN Etain -- but with no memory of her past life. T4: A THOUSAND AND TWELVE YEARS had passed since Etain's original marriage to Midir when she grew up as Etar's daughter. In the mortal Ireland of that time, the HIGH KING was EOCHAID AIREM, and he took Etain to wife not knowing who she was. Midir came in disguise to the royal court of Tara, saw his lost wife again, and challenged the king to a series of games of FIDCHELL (the ancient Irish chess-like board game). T5: Midir let the king win game after game; each time the king named a prize, and each time Midir paid it (mounds of horses, treasures). Then Midir asked for one last game, this time HIS choice of prize -- and this game he won. His prize: to embrace and kiss ETAIN, one time. The king agreed for a month later. When the day came, the king barred every door of Tara with soldiers. Midir simply appeared IN THE HALL, took Etain in his arms, and the two of them flew UP THROUGH THE SKYLIGHT as TWO SWANS, linked by a chain of gold, and were gone forever (Tochmarc Etaine part III). The king Eochaid dug up every sidhe mound in Ireland trying to find her, and never did. Further rungs: the Tochmarc Etaine survives in the Yellow Book of Lecan and the Book of the Dun Cow; it is one of the manuscript pieces that scholars think most preserves genuinely OLD material, some of it dating back to pre-Christian Ireland; the SIR ORFEO Middle-English romance (c. 1330) is a direct descendant of the Etain story, transferred to a British setting; Etain reborn a thousand years later without memory of her first life is the earliest REINCARNATION story in Western literature; the FLY-IN-THE-CUP conception of the second Etain is a motif that reappears in Merlin's conception in Arthurian romance and in the birth of a hundred later heroes.

Best 1938). SCHOLARLY: Tomas O Cathasaigh, 'The Semantics of Sid' (1977); James MacKillop; Proinsias Mac Cana. Middle-English DESCENDANT: Sir Orfeo (Anonymous, c. 1330). Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a jealous DRUIDESS wife turned the rival into a FLY and blew her around Ireland for SEVEN YEARS until she was DRUNK IN A CUP by a woman who then gave birth to her, so she was REBORN as her own daughter A THOUSAND YEARS LATER) and T5 (Midir won her back at a game of FIDCHELL for the price of ONE KISS, and when the king barred every door of Tara, Midir and Etain flew UP THROUGH THE SKYLIGHT AS TWO SWANS chained together in gold). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem summarise the plot AND ask names; describe the SCENE (a jealous first wife turning a rival to a fly, a king playing chess against a stranger, two swans linked by a golden chain flying up through a hall's skylight) and let the recall be MIDIR, ETAIN, or the GAME. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Orpheus and Eurydice, or Cupid and Psyche, or Persephone's return -- a lost-lover-recovered myth. Told without smug-atheist 'primitive belief' framing: this is one of the most sophisticated love-stories in medieval European literature. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Irish love-stories (Aengus and Caer swan-maiden -- adjacent, own ladder; Diarmuid and Grainne -- own ladder in Fionn cycle; Cuchulainn and Fand -- own ladder in Ulster cycle), other 'reborn-a-thousand-years-later' motifs (Fintan mac Bochra the salmon in Lebor Gabala -- adjacent), other 'played chess for a wife' motifs (rare, but the Welsh Mabinogion has an echo). Wrong game: FIDCHELL specifically (Irish 'wood-sense', a chess-like board game).
history_overlap: LITERATURE owns Sir Orfeo (Middle English romance c. 1330) as a poem; theology owns the Irish TOCHMARC ETAINE source it derives from. GEOGRAPHY owns BRI LEITH (Ardagh Mountain in Longford) as a real place; theology owns which god the Irish said lived under it.

name: The Children of Lir: nine hundred years as swans
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: One of the THREE SORROWS OF STORYTELLING of Ireland, from Oidheadh Chlainne Lir ('The Fate of the Children of Lir', ed. Eugene O'Curry 1863). T1: LIR (father of MANANNAN MAC LIR) was a Tuatha De god of the sea. His first wife AOBH (EEV) bore him FOUR CHILDREN -- FIONNUALA (the daughter, and eldest) and her three brothers AODH (EE), CONN, and FIACHRA. When Aobh died, Lir married her sister AOIFE (EE-fa). At first Aoife was a good stepmother to the children. T2: But Aoife grew jealous of how much Lir loved the four children. One day she took them to the lake of DERRAVARAGH in the modern County Westmeath. As they played in the water, she STRUCK THEM WITH A DRUID'S ROD and TURNED ALL FOUR INTO SWANS. She could not undo their voices, though -- they kept their power to SING and to SPEAK IRISH. She could not undo their minds -- they remembered who they were. T3: her curse laid a term on the transformation: they must spend THREE HUNDRED YEARS on Lake Derravaragh; THREE HUNDRED YEARS on the SEA OF MOYLE (the sea between Ireland and Scotland, the roughest of all Irish waters); and THREE HUNDRED MORE YEARS on the ATLANTIC off the ISLE OF INISHGLORA in the west. NINE HUNDRED YEARS in total. The curse could be broken only when a woman of the SOUTH married a man of the NORTH, and when the bells of Christianity rang across Ireland. T4: when Lir found out, he took a druid's rod to Aoife and turned HER into a DEMON OF THE AIR forever after. Lir came to Derravaragh to say goodbye to his children, and every Tuatha De god came with him. For three centuries at Derravaragh the four swans sang so beautifully that a fair was held every year on the shore to hear them. Then they had to fly to the Sea of Moyle, where they suffered three centuries of cold and storm -- Fionnuala had to shelter her three brothers under her wings against the freezing spray. Then three more centuries on the wild Atlantic. T5: at last, after NINE HUNDRED YEARS, the bells of a hermit named MOCHAOMHOG rang out on Inishglora -- the first Christian bells in the west of Ireland. A woman of Munster (the south, married to a Connacht king (the north). The curse broke. The four swans changed back -- but they were now nine hundred years old. They aged in a moment into four ancient wrinkled bodies. Mochaomhog baptised them in Christ before they died, and buried them together, Fionnuala in the middle with her three brothers under her arms as she had sheltered them on the Sea of Moyle. Further rungs: 'The Fate of the Children of Lir' is one of the THREE SORROWS OF STORYTELLING (Tri Truaighe na Scealaigheachta) of medieval Ireland, alongside 'The Fate of the Children of Tuireann' (which turns on Lugh's family) and 'The Fate of the Children of Uisneach' (Deirdre of the Sorrows); the story is the source of the Irish national tenderness for SWANS -- to this day it is illegal in Ireland to shoot a swan; a bronze SCULPTURE of the four swan-children by Oisin Kelly stands in the Garden of Remembrance in Parnell Square, Dublin, in memory of those who died for Irish freedom; the story's Christian ending -- the swan-children baptised at the moment of death -- is a beautiful example of Irish myth's SYNCRETISM with the incoming Church.

framing_note: The CHILDREN OF LIR ladder -- one of the sorrows, kids remember it forever. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (NINE HUNDRED YEARS as swans -- 300 on a peaceful lake, 300 on the freezing Sea of Moyle where the SISTER SHELTERED her brothers under her wings against the storms, 300 on the wild Atlantic) and T5 (when they finally CHANGED BACK, they were NINE HUNDRED YEARS OLD and aged instantly into four ancient bodies -- baptised at the moment of death and buried together). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'four children turned to swans' AND ask their story; describe the SCENE (a jealous stepmother striking with a druid's rod, four swans on a lake with human voices, a sister sheltering three brothers under her wings against sea-spray) and let the recall be the CHILDREN OF LIR, the NUMBER of years, or the SISTER'S name Fionnuala. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Snow White's dwarves mourning, or the Norse Balder's funeral, or the death of Roland at Roncesvalles -- a great mythic sorrow. The Christian ending (baptism at the moment of aged death) is presented as historical syncretism, not as a doctrinal payoff. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Irish swan-stories (Aengus and Caer swan-maiden -- own ladder; Cuchulainn's Fand -- other cycle), other 'cursed for hundreds of years' motifs (Oisin in Tir na nOg -- own Fionn ladder; the Wandering Jew -- other pillar), other 'three sorrows' (Deirdre of the Sorrows -- Ulster cycle; the Children of Tuireann -- own ladder). name: The Fir Bolg: the bag-men and the five provinces
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The FOURTH invasion of Ireland and the wave the Tuatha De Danann displaced, from Lebor Gabala Erenn. T1: before the Tuatha De Danann came to Ireland, the country was held by the FIR BOLG -- the FOURTH wave of settlers in the Book of Invasions. They were descendants of the earlier Nemedians who had fled Ireland after the Fomorian raids reduced them to thirty survivors. T2: their name means 'the BAG MEN'. The Book of Invasions gives a folk-etymology: the survivors of the Nemedians had fled to GREECE, where they were enslaved and made to CARRY EARTH IN LEATHER BAGS from the fertile lowlands up onto rocky hillsides to build farmland for their Greek masters. When they escaped, they used their earth-bags to make hide BOATS and sailed home to Ireland. Hence FIR BOLG, 'MEN OF THE BAGS'. (This is folk-etymology; the older meaning of 'Bolg' is probably 'BELGAE', the same name as the Continental Celtic Belgae after whom Belgium is named.) T3: the Fir Bolg's great contribution to Ireland was the DIVISION OF THE ISLAND INTO PROVINCES. Their king SLAINGE mac Dela divided Ireland into FIVE COIGEDA ('fifths' -- CUIG in modern Irish, meaning 'FIVE') -- ULSTER in the north, LEINSTER in the east, MUNSTER in the south, CONNACHT in the west, and MIDE (Meath) in the sacred CENTRE. These five provinces are still the traditional divisions of Ireland today, though modern political Ireland has only four provinces (Mide having been absorbed into Leinster). T4: when the Tuatha De Danann arrived in dark clouds, the two peoples fought the FIRST BATTLE OF MOYTURA (Cath Maige Tuired Cunga) on the plain of Cong in Mayo. It was there that SRENG, the Fir Bolg champion, cut off Nuada's hand with one sword-stroke (see the Nuada ladder). The Tuatha De won, but respectfully -- the surviving Fir Bolg were offered any one of the five provinces to keep for themselves. They chose CONNACHT, the west, and lived there ever after. T5: the Fir Bolg do not disappear from Irish myth. Later legend makes several great Ulster and Connacht families their DESCENDANTS -- the connection is fictional but was proudly claimed. In the Tain Bo Cuailnge (the Cattle-Raid of Cooley), the great Connacht champion FERGUS MAC ROICH is sometimes said to be of Fir Bolg descent, and QUEEN MEDB of Connacht (Cuchulainn's opponent) rules from Cruachan in what had been the Fir Bolg province. So the Fir Bolg quietly persist as an ancestor-line woven through later Irish literature. Further rungs: the FIFTH invasion after the Fir Bolg is the Tuatha De Danann; the SIXTH is the Milesians (see the six-invasions ladder); King SLAINGE mac Dela is said to be the first Irish king to die of natural causes -- all before him were killed in battle or plague; the reduction from FIVE to FOUR provinces (with MIDE dropping out) happened gradually over the medieval period and was politically complete by 1152; the great earthen fortress of RATH CROGHAN in Roscommon, capital of Connacht, is traditionally the Fir Bolg royal seat.

name: The Fomorians: sea-monster people, one-legged and one-eyed
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The primordial enemies of every Irish invasion, and the villains of the Second Battle of Moytura. T1: the FOMORIANS (Old Irish FOMOIRE, pronounced FOM-or-uh) are the ancient DARK RACE of Irish myth -- sea-raiders and monsters who inhabited Ireland (or the waters and rocky islands around Ireland) BEFORE any of the six waves of settlers arrived, and who continued to attack each incoming wave. Their name is thought to mean 'UNDER-DEMONS' or 'UNDER-SEA ONES' (fo = under, mor = sea). T2: the Fomorians are described in the Book of Invasions as MISSHAPEN -- many of them had only ONE EYE, ONE ARM, or ONE LEG. They were vast, brutish, and cruel. Their strongholds were the wild islands off the west coast of Ireland, especially TORY ISLAND off Donegal (Balor's fortress), the ARAN ISLANDS, and the CLIFFS OF MOHER. T3: the Fomorians were the enemies of the second wave (PARTHOLON -- who they nearly wiped out), the third wave (NEMED -- whose people they reduced to thirty survivors and whom they forced to pay a TRIBUTE of two-thirds of their children and grain every SAMHAIN, delivered to the tower of CONAND on Tory Island), and finally the fifth wave (the TUATHA DE DANANN). They imposed the same tribute on the Tuatha De under the tyranny of BRES (see the Bres ladder). T4: at the SECOND BATTLE OF MOYTURA (Cath Maige Tuired, on the plain of Moytura in County Sligo), the Tuatha De Danann under Lugh, Nuada, and the Dagda faced the Fomorians under BALOR of the Evil Eye and INDECH mac De Domnann. Nuada was killed by Balor's gaze; Lugh killed Balor with a sling-stone through the eye (see the Balor ladder); the Fomorians were BROKEN utterly and driven back to the sea. The Fomorians never troubled Ireland again as a fighting force. T5: several great Tuatha De heroes were of MIXED Fomorian and Tuatha blood -- BRES (mother Eriu Tuatha, father Elatha Fomorian), LUGH himself (father Cian Tuatha, mother Ethlinn daughter of Balor Fomorian). So the war between the peoples was also (as in many mythologies -- Aesir vs Jotnar in Norse, Olympians vs Titans in Greek) a FAMILY WAR, brothers and grandsons on opposing sides. Some scholars read the Fomorians as symbolizing WINTER, DARKNESS, CHAOS, and SEA-STORMS against the Tuatha De as HARVEST, LIGHT, ORDER, and GOOD-EARTH farming -- the eternal cosmic struggle in an Irish key. Further rungs: the exact word FOMOIRE is Old Irish and its cognates appear in other Celtic languages -- the Welsh AFANC (water-monster) may share an origin; the Norse JOTNAR are the closest structural parallel across pillars -- primordial giants who fight the gods; the modern Aran Islanders still tell stories in which the Fomorians built the great STONE FORTS (Dun Aengus and Dun Duchathair) on their cliffs, though archaeology dates the forts to the Iron Age; the surviving Fomorians (after Moytura) are said in some sources to have been ABSORBED into the Tuatha De through intermarriage and quietly disappear from later tradition.
