name: The Milesians and Amergin's poem: 'I am a wind on the sea'
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The sixth and final wave of settlers to Ireland, and the poem their druid sang as he stepped ashore. T1: the MILESIANS -- the sons of MIL ESPAINE ('Mil of Spain') -- were the SIXTH and LAST wave in the Book of Invasions. They came from SPAIN, or more precisely (in the legendary geography) from GALICIA in the north-west. They were the ancestors of the modern Irish Gaels, and every Irish person alive today is descended (in the mythic frame) from a Milesian son. T2: their coming was PROPHESIED. The Tuatha De Danann's three eponymous queens -- ERIU, BANBA, and FODLA -- met the Milesians as they marched inland. Each queen asked that Ireland be NAMED FOR HER. AMERGIN, the Milesian druid-poet, promised each queen her name -- but ERIU's name would be the one used in daily speech, and EIRE (Ireland) is her name to this day. Banba and Fodla survive as poetic names for Ireland in Irish literature. T3: the Tuatha De then used druid-magic to raise a great MAGIC WIND that drove the Milesian ships nine waves back out to sea, hoping to prevent their landing. AMERGIN GLUINGEL ('WHITE-KNEED AMERGIN'), the Milesian chief-druid, out-magicked them. Standing on the deck of his ship, he chanted a poem that CALMED THE WIND, and then he stepped onto the Irish shore and sang another poem to CLAIM the land. T4: the poem Amergin sang stepping ashore is one of the OLDEST surviving pieces of Irish literature. Its opening lines: 'I AM A WIND ON THE SEA, / I AM A WAVE OF THE OCEAN, / I AM THE ROAR OF THE SEA, / I AM A STAG OF SEVEN TINES, / I AM A HAWK ON A CLIFF, / I AM A TEARDROP OF THE SUN, / I AM FAIR AMONG FLOWERS, / I AM A BOAR FOR VALOUR, / I AM A SALMON IN A POOL, / I AM A LAKE ON A PLAIN, / I AM A WORD OF ART, / I AM A SPEAR-POINT THAT POURS OUT COMBAT, / I AM THE GOD WHO SHAPES FIRE FOR A HEAD' (Amergin Gluingel, preserved in Lebor Gabala Erenn and the Book of Leinster). T5: the Milesians defeated the Tuatha De Danann in battle -- but the sons of Mil, wise enough to know they were fighting gods, offered a DIVISION. The MILESIANS would take the SURFACE of Ireland -- the land, the sea, the sky. The TUATHA DE DANANN would take the UNDERGROUND -- all the sidhe mounds, every hollow-hill and fairy-fort across Ireland. MANANNAN MAC LIR (the sea-god of the Tuatha De) divided the mounds among his people; each god got one. That is how the Milesians (the modern Irish) came to hold the visible island, and how the Tuatha De became the AOS SI, the FAIRY FOLK who live beneath the hills. Further rungs: AMERGIN's poem is often called 'the Song of Amergin' and every Celtic revival writer (W.B. Yeats, Robert Graves in The White Goddess) translated it; the promise that Ireland would be named for ERIU is why Ireland's Irish-language name is EIRE (the modern Republic of Ireland's official name); the Milesians are traced in the Lebor Gabala genealogy back to a NOAHIC ancestor called FENIUS FARSAID, who is said to have created the IRISH LANGUAGE at the Tower of Babel -- another medieval Christian-Irish syncretism; the DINDSHENCHAS ('lore of places') genre of Irish literature is one long footnote to the Milesian claim to the land -- every hill in Ireland has a story of how a Milesian named it.

Dinner-test payoff: T4 (a druid stepping onto a beach and singing 'I AM A WIND ON THE SEA, I AM A WAVE OF THE OCEAN, I AM A STAG OF SEVEN TINES' -- one of the oldest surviving poems in the Irish language) and T5 (the settlement was a DIVISION -- Milesians take the SURFACE, Tuatha De take EVERY HOLLOW HILL, which is how the fairy folk came to live underground). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Aeneas landing in Italy after prophecy, or Moses on the mountain overlooking the Promised Land -- a founding-people arrival, treated with full mythic seriousness. DISTRACTOR MINE: other invasion-waves (Cessair, Partholon, Nemed, Fir Bolg, Tuatha De -- keep straight, own six-invasions ladder), other 'I am' identity-poems (Christ's 'I am the way and the truth and the life' -- other pillar; the Welsh Taliesin poems -- adjacent Celtic tradition), other 'named for a queen' motifs (Athena and Athens -- other pillar; Roma and Rome -- other pillar). Wrong number of queens: THREE Tuatha De queens (Eriu, Banba, Fodla), not two, not four.

name: Newgrange: Aengus tricks the Dagda out of Bru na Boinne
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The mythic origin story of Ireland's most famous ancient monument. T1: BRU NA BOINNE ('the palace of the BOYNE') is the ancient passage-tomb known today as NEWGRANGE, on a bend of the RIVER BOYNE in County Meath. It was built around 3200 BC -- MAKING IT OLDER THAN THE EGYPTIAN PYRAMIDS BY 500 YEARS. In Irish myth it was the dwelling of the DAGDA, chief of the Tuatha De Danann. T2: the Dagda had built the Bru with the help of ELCMAR (a rival Tuatha De god who officially owned the site and lived there). The Dagda then fell in love with BOANN, Elcmar's wife (and goddess of the River Boyne). The Dagda sent Elcmar away on an errand and enchanted the daylight so that a SINGLE DAY LASTED NINE MONTHS. During that endless day the Dagda and Boann conceived a son -- AENGUS. When Elcmar returned, thinking only a day had passed, the child was already born and hidden away in fosterage. T3: Aengus grew up not knowing his father. When he learned the truth, he came to the Dagda and asked for a portion of land like every other Tuatha De god had. The Dagda answered that all the land had already been divided; there was nothing left. So Aengus (advised by MANANNAN or, in some sources, by MIDIR) played a trick. He asked the Dagda if he could stay at BRU NA BOINNE 'FOR A DAY AND A NIGHT' (LA OCUS OIDCHE in Old Irish). The Dagda agreed. T4: when the day and night were up, the Dagda asked for the Bru back. Aengus answered with a piece of Old Irish grammatical logic: 'LA OCUS OIDCHE' can mean 'a day and a night' OR (with a different reading of the definite article) 'DAY AND NIGHT' -- that is, ALL DAYS AND ALL NIGHTS FOREVER. Under Irish law of the word, once a claim was made in that form and accepted, it stood. The Dagda was TRICKED OUT OF HIS OWN PALACE by his son's wordplay. Aengus took possession of Bru na Boinne and held it thereafter (Tochmarc Etaine part I; De Gabail in tSida). T5: the whole story is preserved in the Metrical Dindshenchas as the origin-tale of the great stone monument still standing on the Boyne. The passage inside Newgrange is 19 metres long and aligned so that on the WINTER SOLSTICE morning (December 21), the sunrise SHINES DOWN THE PASSAGE and illuminates the inner chamber for exactly 17 minutes -- the ONE DAY OF THE YEAR the god's tomb is lit from within. Every year a lottery decides which few people get to be inside on those seventeen minutes; the world watches by livestream. Neolithic Ireland built the monument, but medieval Ireland attached the myth: the light entering the passage at winter solstice is the god AENGUS receiving his father's palace, or (in another reading) the SUN visiting the LOVER inside the tomb-womb of BOANN. Further rungs: the Boyne complex also includes KNOWTH and DOWTH, two other great passage-tombs of similar age; the RIVER BOYNE is named after BOANN, who (in her own origin story) approached the sacred well of SEGAIS to test its wisdom, and the well surged up and drowned her, her body carried out to sea -- becoming the river; the CLEVER-YOUNG-SON-TRICKS-OLD-FATHER motif is one of Irish myth's most persistent shapes, echoing in later stories from Cormac mac Airt to Fionn mac Cumhaill.

SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Jacob tricking Esau out of the birthright with lentil stew, or Loki's wordplay-tricks in Norse myth -- clever-youth-outwits-elder is a universal pattern. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Tuatha De sidhe mounds (the Dagda at Bru na Boinne originally; Midir at Bri Leith; Manannan on the Isle of Man; Bodb Derg in Munster -- keep straight), other Neolithic monuments (Stonehenge -- other pillar; Knowth and Dowth -- adjacent, part of the same Boyne complex), other trickster-inheritance stories (Jacob and Esau -- Christian pillar; Loki -- Norse pillar). name: The Sidhe Mounds and the Aos Si: where the gods went underground
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: How the Tuatha De Danann became the fairy folk of Irish folklore. T1: after the MILESIANS defeated the Tuatha De Danann (the SIXTH wave defeating the FIFTH, see the invasions ladders), the two sides settled by DIVISION. The Milesians took the SURFACE of Ireland -- everything a human eye could see. The Tuatha De took the UNDERGROUND -- every hollow hill, every green mound, every ancient cairn scattered across Ireland. T2: from that day the Tuatha De Danann are called the AOS SI (EES SHEE) -- 'the PEOPLE OF THE MOUNDS' -- or, in English, the FAIRY FOLK. The mounds themselves are the SIDHE (SHEE), and each mound is a gateway to the OTHERWORLD, an eternal country underneath Ireland that runs by different time and different laws. The word SIDHE lives on in modern Irish as SI, still meaning 'fairy-mound' or 'the fairy folk'. T3: MANANNAN MAC LIR, the sea-god of the Tuatha De, MANAGED THE DIVISION of the mounds. He gave one mound to each of the great gods -- AENGUS got BRU NA BOINNE (Newgrange, see that ladder), MIDIR got BRI LEITH (Ardagh Mountain in County Longford), the DAGDA got a mound above the Boyne, BODB DERG got a mound in Munster, LIR got a mound near the sea. Manannan also gave them the FEAST OF GOIBNIU (a magical never-ending feast that keeps the gods young) and the PIGS OF MANANNAN (which can be killed and eaten and are alive again the next morning). T4: to CROSS INTO A SIDHE MOUND is to leave time. Mortal visitors return after what feels like a night to find HUNDREDS OF YEARS have passed above ground -- the classic case is OISIN son of Fionn who spent 300 years in TIR NA NOG and turned to dust the moment his foot touched Irish earth again (see the Fionn / Oisin ladder). SAMHAIN (November 1) is the night the sidhe mounds OPEN and the two worlds mingle -- ancestor of the modern HALLOWEEN. On Samhain the ghosts of the dead walk out and the aos si walk in. T5: the SIDHE never leave Ireland. In modern folk tradition every county still knows its FAIRY FORTS (small round earthworks -- prehistoric ring-forts) and its FAIRY TREES (usually solitary hawthorns) which MUST NOT BE DISTURBED, ploughed, or cut down. As late as 1999, an entire ROAD PROJECT in County Clare was re-routed to spare a single hawthorn tree said to belong to the sidhe -- because the construction workers refused to touch it. The gods still hold their mounds after three thousand years. Further rungs: the BANSHEE (BEAN-SIDHE, 'woman of the mounds') is a survival of the aos si -- a fairy-woman who wails at a house whose head is about to die, a folk-echo of the Morrigan as Washer at the Ford; PUCA (a shape-shifting mischievous fairy who can be black horse, hare, or man) is another aos si descendant; the LEPRECHAUN (LUCHORPAN, 'small body') is a diminished sidhe cobbler; every one of these Irish folk-figures is a Tuatha De god in retreat; the Otherworld under the mounds has many names -- TIR NA NOG (the Land of Youth), MAG MELL (the Plain of Delights), EMAIN ABLACH (the Isle of Apples), TIR TAIRNGIRE (the Land of Promise) -- overlapping regions of the same undying country.

Acallam na Senorach ('The Colloquy of the Ancients', 12th c. -- Oisin returning to a Christianised Ireland after time in Tir na nOg). Metrical Dindshenchas. name: Boann and the River Boyne: the well of Segais
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: How Ireland's River Boyne got its name -- from a goddess drowned by a sacred well. T1: BOANN (BOO-an) is a river-goddess of the Tuatha De Danann, wife of the god ELCMAR and later lover of the DAGDA. She is the mother of AENGUS (see the Newgrange ladder for that story). Her name means 'the WHITE COW' (bo-fhinn), and she is the goddess of the RIVER BOYNE (An Bhoinn) that runs past Newgrange in County Meath. T2: the story of how the river came to be is told in the Metrical Dindshenchas ('lore of places') -- one of the great Irish place-name origin-tales. In the DAYS OF THE TUATHA DE DANANN, there stood in the middle of Ireland a SACRED WELL called SEGAIS. Around the well grew NINE HAZEL TREES OF WISDOM -- the SAME hazel trees whose nuts, dropping into the salmon-pools, gave the SALMON OF KNOWLEDGE its wisdom (see the Fionn / Salmon of Knowledge ladder, and note the whole-country hydrological cycle: hazel nuts feed the Boyne salmon, the Boyne feeds the sea). T3: only certain PERMITTED persons -- the well's guardian NECHTAN and his three cup-bearers -- could safely approach the Well of Segais. Everyone else was FORBIDDEN to go near it, on pain of the water rising against them. Boann, whose husband Elcmar was somehow related to Nechtan, was FORBIDDEN. T4: Boann came to the well anyway, walking three times COUNTER-SUNWISE around it as an act of DEFIANCE (or, in another version, testing whether the taboo was real). The waters ROSE UP AGAINST HER -- burst out of the well in a great flood, chased her down the plain of Meath, tore off her eye, her arm, and her leg (a triple bodily-perfection-broken echo, see Nuada), and drowned her. The water kept running: it became the RIVER BOYNE, still flowing today from that same source, out through Meath, past Newgrange, and into the Irish Sea (Metrical Dindshenchas of Boann). T5: the story is a mythic ETIOLOGY -- an origin-story -- for Ireland's second-longest river, and for the SACREDNESS of the Boyne valley as a whole. Newgrange (Bru na Boinne, 'palace of the Boyne') is named for her. Knowth and Dowth stand on her banks. Boann's death is not a punishment -- it is a TRANSFIGURATION: the goddess becomes the river, and every drop of water in the Boyne is (in the mythic reading) her. Every salmon fished from the Boyne carries her wisdom; every ancient tomb on her banks is her house. Further rungs: the WELL OF SEGAIS as sacred source appears in other Irish tales -- SINANN, another Tuatha De woman, meets the same fate at a DIFFERENT sacred well and BECOMES the RIVER SHANNON (Ireland's LONGEST river), by exactly parallel means; the Well of Segais motif -- hazel wisdom, forbidden waters, transfigured goddess -- may descend from a shared Indo-European mythic pattern (the Norse well of Urdr under Yggdrasil has similar shape); the modern Irish word 'BOINN' still refers to the river, and the county of MEATH takes its cultural centre from her valley.

name: Nuada's death at Moytura and Lugh's kingship
strand: Western myth: Irish mythology -- Tuatha De Danann and the Mythological Cycle
scope: The Second Battle of Moytura -- the war that decides the fate of the Tuatha De Danann. T1: after Nuada was restored to the throne (his flesh-hand regrown by Miach, see the Nuada ladder), and after Lugh arrived at Tara as the Ildanach (see the doorkeeper ladder), the Tuatha De Danann prepared for the great war against the Fomorians. Nuada VOLUNTARILY YIELDED the throne to Lugh for THIRTEEN DAYS before the battle -- 'it was easier that a king should stand in for a champion than that a champion stand in for a king' (Cath Maige Tuired sec 74). Lugh took command of the battle-preparation. T2: the SECOND BATTLE OF MOYTURA (Cath Maige Tuired, 'the battle of the plain of pillars') was fought on the plain of MOYTURA in County Sligo -- the same region where the Morrigan's ford of the Unius runs (see the Morrigan ladder). On the eve of battle, the Dagda kept his tryst with the Morrigan at the ford; she promised the Tuatha De 'the blood from the heart of the Fomorian king Indech'. T3: the battle went badly at first. NUADA of the Silver Hand, the true king, met BALOR of the Evil Eye on the battlefield. Balor's four warriors lifted his poison eyelid, and Balor's gaze CUT DOWN NUADA and Nuada's wife MACHA (one of the Morrigan-triad) with him. Nuada, the first king of the Tuatha De in Ireland, DIED IN THE PRIME OF HIS RESTORED MANHOOD. The Tuatha De reeled at the loss of their king. T4: LUGH stepped up. Lugh was actually forbidden by his guardians from being on the battlefield -- 'they set nine warriors to guard him behind the ranks, for he was too valuable to risk in single combat'. But Lugh SLIPPED HIS GUARD, ran to the front, and confronted Balor. As Balor's eyelid was lifting, Lugh cast a stone from his SLING (or a spear -- accounts vary; some name it the Spear of Assal from Gorias) that struck Balor's eye and drove out the back of his head, killing him and turning the gaze back on the Fomorian ranks. The Fomorians were broken (see the Balor ladder). T5: after the victory, LUGH was made KING of the Tuatha De Danann in Nuada's place -- and he ruled for FORTY YEARS. Bres (see that ladder) was spared, but was brought before Lugh in chains and, to save his own life, taught the Tuatha De the SECRETS OF PLOUGHING and SOWING and HARVESTING that the Fomorians had guarded from them until then. Lugh's reign was the golden age of the Tuatha De Danann in Ireland -- until, generations later, the Milesians came and it all ended (see the invasions ladders). Lugh himself is said in some sources to have died drowned in Loch Lugborta by three sons of Cermait avenging their father -- see the further rungs. Further rungs: Lugh's death (killed in vengeance by the three sons of the Dagda's son Cermait, whom Lugh had earlier slain for adultery with his own wife) is preserved in a short obscure tale; the harvest festival LUGHNASADH (August 1) is founded by Lugh in memory of his foster-mother TAILTIU, who had died clearing the plains of Ireland for agriculture; the DAGDA also died at Moytura, from a wound inflicted by the Fomorian queen CETHLENN (Balor's wife) -- he outlived the battle but succumbed later.

Dinner-test payoff: T3 (NUADA the KING, restored to a flesh hand and back on the throne, was KILLED by BALOR'S POISON GAZE early in the battle, along with his wife MACHA the Morrigan-triad member) and T4 (LUGH SLIPPED HIS OWN GUARDS to get to the front and killed his grandfather with a sling-stone through the eye). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem summarize the battle AND ask outcome; describe the SCENE (a first king killed early in the battle, a young champion breaking away from his guards, a sling and a poison-eyed grandfather) and let the recall be NUADA, LUGH, or the specific NAMED DEATH. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Ragnarok in Norse, or the fall of Troy in Greek, or the Passion in Christian pillar -- a mythic-scale battle where a whole world hangs on the outcome. DISTRACTOR MINE: FIRST vs SECOND battles of Moytura (First = Tuatha De vs Fir Bolg, Nuada loses hand; Second = Tuatha De vs Fomorians, Nuada dies), other 'young champion slips his guardians' motifs (Achilles at Troy, young David at Goliath -- other pillars), other named deaths at Moytura (Nuada, Macha, the Dagda-wounded-later, Ogma -- keep straight). Wrong king-succession: NUADA -> BRES (briefly) -> NUADA (restored) -> LUGH (13 days before battle + full kingship after) -> the Dagda later -> and eventually the last Tuatha De king Mac Cuill, Mac Cecht, and Mac Greine (who lose to the Milesians).
